newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN PM SAYS SCANDAL NO DIRECT PROBLEM FOR GOVT.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN PM SAYS SCANDAL NO DIRECT PROBLEM FOR GOVT.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene said there were "no direct problems" at the heart of his four-party coaltion government, under pressure from a corruption scandal involving one partner, the Francophone socialists.
In an interview in Belgium's L'Echo newspaper published on Friday Dehaene also appeared to rule out early elections, reiterating that the government's term ran until 1999.

Asked whether he felt he could rely on French-speaking PS socialist party as a coalition partner and about calls by the opposition PRL liberal party to change the coalition he firmly said, "I have a government agreement."
"If there is quarrelling between the parties, let them resolve that between themselves. I see no repercussions (or) direct problems at the heart of the government," he added.
"I have a government programme for which I need the whole of the political term of office."

Belgium's government will face a vote of no confidence next week after the erruption of the bribes-for-contracts scandal implicating French defence firm Dassault . Dassault has denied all wrong doing.

In recent days two former senior PS officials have been arrested and charged of corruption in the affair. A former Belgian army colonel has also been charged on the same count and legal moves to start questioning a former leader of the PS are underway.

Asked if the political parties were in a predicament over the Dassault affair because they all had something to reproach themselves for, Dehaene said there had been problems generally with party financing because, before a 1989 law, some gifts to parties were legal and there had been "grey areas".

"What we are talking about now happened before the law of 1989....," he said adding that the allegations made in the Dassault affair "do not interfere at all in the way policy is carried out and the way the parties work today," Dehaene said.
However he added that the judiciary must do its job and bribes for contracts "never have been and never will be legal."
